question: Tell me about a time you stopped polishing because delivery mattered more. How did you decide?
competency: Relentlessly push boundaries (knowing when to ship vs. perfect)

raiseTranscript.text: I was building a reporting dashboard for my team. After the core queries and charts worked, I kept tweaking the layout and colors. My manager flagged that stakeholders needed the data for a quarterly review in two days.

I listed the remaining polish items, estimated another three days, and realized the data itself was accurate. I shipped the functional version and noted the UI tweaks as follow-up. The team used it on time.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you stopped polishing because delivery mattered more. How did you decide?
Role: Individual contributor on internal dashboard
Situation: Core data ready, UI still being iterated
Action: Listed remaining items, compared to deadline, shipped functional version
Outcome: Team met quarterly review date
Quote: "I realized the data itself was accurate."
Follow-up: How did you know the data was accurate enough? Candidate: Ran the same queries against source tables and matched totals.
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Relentlessly push boundaries. Junior candidate described stopping UI polish on an internal dashboard once core queries were verified. They explicitly compared remaining work (three days) against a hard stakeholder deadline and chose to ship. The decision stayed within their individual scope and showed they could weigh trade-offs without being told. Biggest strength is the concrete stopping criterion tied to an external date rather than vague "good enough" language.

lowerTranscript.text: I was working on a feature and kept fixing small bugs because I wanted it to be really solid. My manager eventually told me to just hand it over.
What signal made you realize you should have stopped earlier?
I didn't really have one. I just thought more fixes would make it better until the deadline passed.

Biggest gap is absence of any decision criteria the candidate owned.

raiseTranscript.text: Our team was launching a shared API used by three other squads. We had a list of edge-case error messages still in progress. Two days before the agreed launch window, one partner team said their integration was blocked until we shipped.
How did you decide what to cut?

I pulled the three squads into a quick sync, ranked the open items by blast radius, and moved two low-impact messages to post-launch. We documented the gaps and shipped the core contract on the original date.

Follow-up: What happened to the deferred items? Candidate: Tracked them in the next sprint and closed within two weeks.
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Relentlessly push boundaries. Senior candidate described a cross-team API launch where they facilitated a ranking session across three squads to defer low-impact items. The decision used explicit criteria (blast radius) and protected the launch date while documenting trade-offs. Story shows influence without authority and measurable coordination impact. Biggest strength is the repeatable process they used to align multiple teams on the cut line.

lowerTranscript.text: We had an API launch and kept adding more validation because we wanted it robust. The other teams started complaining about the delay so we eventually shipped what we had.
How did you decide which validation could wait?
I didn't run a formal review. We just felt the pressure and cut the last two items the day before launch.

raiseTranscript.text: We were six weeks from a new market launch that the board had tied to annual revenue targets. The product still had two major reliability gaps. I asked the team to run a forced ranking against the revenue model and customer commitments.

We moved one reliability feature to a day-two release, accepted a monitored degradation in one region, and launched on schedule. Post-launch we recovered the feature in four weeks and hit the revenue number.
